description: We are The Celestials, and we are open to all: any background and any skill level is welcome. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge we're building a web tool. To count for global judging, teammates must be registered for the Columbus, GA local event.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool for watching the infrared sky change. Enter any sky position or object name and it fetches NASA SPHEREx images of that patch from every survey pass, lines them up, and blinks them like a short video, so anything that moved or changed brightness stands out. In false colour, ordinary stars are white and cold objects such as brown dwarfs glow red. Click any object to get its infrared spectrum and its brightness over time, measured on the spot. A WISE image from 2010 can join the blink, which stretches the time span from one year to fifteen. A candidate finder then lists what moved, what changed, and what no catalogue explains.

It answers the challenge directly: coordinates in, a little video out, read live from NASA's archive, so new data releases appear with no rebuild. Tested on all five challenge targets, it measured Barnard's Star moving 9.95 arcseconds per year (Gaia says 10.39).

SPHEREx returns images of more than a billion objects, and no one person can look through them alone. A tool that lets anyone check a patch of sky in a minute opens the search for the Sun's cold, faint neighbours to everyone.
details:
Live tool: https://spherex-blink.azurewebsites.net. Code: https://github.com/Darskye/spherex-blink. The live site runs on free hosting: the first page after a quiet spell can take a minute or two to wake, and the site rests if its daily allowance runs out. The code runs on any computer with the three commands in the README.

What it does

  • Enter RA and Dec (decimal or sexagesimal) or an object name. The tool finds every SPHEREx exposure of that spot, aligns the images north-up, combines each survey pass, and blinks the passes with play, step, speed, zoom and pan.
  • Colour view builds three broad channels from the six detectors (0.75 to 5.0 µm), balanced so ordinary stars are white and cold objects are red.
  • Difference mode subtracts the first pass from each later one. Sum mode adds everything together.
  • Click any source to get its spectrum (one point per exposure, at the wavelength that exposure sampled), its brightness over time, and its measured motion in arcseconds per year.
  • "Compare with 2010" adds the WISE mission's image of the same field to the blink, a 15-year baseline.
  • Gaia DR3 stars are drawn where they were on each frame's date, with arrows on fast movers. Click anything and "What is it?" gives its name and type from SIMBAD, 2MASS and AllWISE, or says that no catalogue has anything there.
  • Flagged pixels can be overlaid, and measurements that are saturated or blended with a neighbour are marked and explained.
  • Every view is a link (the coordinates are in the address), and an embed option gives an iframe.
  • The candidate finder measures every source in every pass and lists what moved, what changed brightness, what no catalogue lists, and what a 2010 catalogue lists that is not there now. It works by measurement alone and consults the catalogues only afterwards.
  • Simulate mode runs the clock forward or back by moving each star by its measured motion. It is labelled as a simulation, not an observation.

How it works

  • One Python service (FastAPI) serves both the API and the page. The page is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no libraries and no build step.
  • Nothing is pre-made. Each view asks NASA's IRSA archive which exposures cover the position, downloads small cutouts, and caches them, so a return visit downloads only what is new.
  • Each cutout file is about 4 MB, but the parts the viewer needs are the first 130 to 200 kB. The download stops there, which makes loading far faster and is kinder to the archive.
  • Frames reach the browser as raw numbers and are stretched, coloured, blinked and subtracted there, so the controls respond at once.
  • SPHEREx sees each object at a different wavelength in each exposure. Measuring the object in every exposure therefore gives its spectrum.

Results on the five challenge targets (measured from public SPHEREx data on 13 Nov 2026)

  • Barnard's Star: hops north between three passes. Measured motion 9.95 ± 0.61 arcseconds per year; Gaia DR3 gives 10.39.
  • Epsilon Indi B: a red dot among white stars. Measured motion about 4.5 ± 0.3 arcseconds per year; the catalogue value is 4.68. Its spectrum shows the brown-dwarf peaks near 1.3, 1.6, 2.1 and 4.0 µm.
  • WISE 0855−0714: a faint red dot at its predicted position, brightest at 4 to 5 µm. It is now blended with a background star, and the tool says so and reports no motion or light curve for it.
  • RW Aurigae: between Sep 2025 and Sep 2026 it brightened by roughly half at 0.9 µm while fading by about 46% at 4 µm.
  • R Draconis: too bright for SPHEREx, so the tool follows it through its unsaturated outer light. That shows a 45% change in the longest-wavelength band between Feb and May 2026.
  • Brightness check: for 9 isolated stars the tool's measurements matched the 2MASS and WISE catalogues to a median ratio of 1.02 with 4% scatter.

The candidate finder, tested

  • Blind test: by measurement alone it finds all five challenge targets, and raises no false alarms in their fields.
  • 100 random fields (about one square degree of sky): 3,869 sources measured, 147 first-look flags, 146 rejected by the tool's own checks. The one that remained is a known quasar now at half its 2010 brightness. Nothing new was found, and we say so. Findings are candidates, not discoveries.

What is creative about it

  • False colour that makes cold objects stand out at a glance.
  • A 15-year baseline from one year of SPHEREx data, by adding WISE to the blink.
  • It recognises old coordinates. The WISE 0855 position in the challenge statement is where the object was around 2010, two arcminutes from where it is now; the tool says so and offers the current position.
  • Stars too bright to measure are followed through their outer light instead of being dropped.

Benefits and intended impact

Anyone with a browser can check a patch of sky in about a minute: students, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists. A link to a view can be shared or embedded in a lesson. We hope it lowers the cost of a first look, so that more eyes go over the SPHEREx sky.

What we considered

  • Honesty about limits. SPHEREx pixels are 6 arcseconds and the survey is about a year old, so even the fastest stars move one or two pixels. The measurements are quick looks, not calibrated science.
  • A distant planet would probably not be found this way: it would be too faint for SPHEREx and would shift out of a small field between passes. The tool is aimed at nearby cold stars and brown dwarfs.
  • Being polite to the archive: few connections, patient retries, and a cache.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Pillow, pytest (49 offline tests), and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Hosted on Azure App Service (free tier).

Use of AI

Built with AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code. The code, tests and visual design were written with Claude under the team's direction; every source file says so in its header, and the README has a "Use of AI" section. Every image the tool shows is real SPHEREx or WISE data. The team logo is AI-generated and is marked as such.
